onboarding.whyNotApiTitle: Why can’t this app connect to Apple Music or Spotify for me?
onboarding.whyNotApiBody: Those companies don’t give independent apps direct access to your personal streaming history — that data stays between you and them, which protects your privacy. We’re a third-party app, so there’s no supported “log in and sync” path for your full history. The official option is for you to request your own copy from their privacy tools; you then import that file here.
onboarding.welcomeBody: We’ll walk you through it. The official export can take a few days — come back when your file is ready.
onboarding.welcomeNoteStrong: You'll import when the ZIP or CSV arrives in your inbox
onboarding.welcomeNoteRest: — exports take time to generate, and that's OK.

spotify.step1Body: On “Download your data”, select Extended streaming history, then tap Request data. It can take up to 30 days.
spotify.step2Body: A green banner confirms Spotify is preparing your file. You’ll get an email when it’s ready.

apple.step1Body: Sign in at privacy.apple.com, then open “Request a copy of your data”.
apple.step2Body: Check Apple Media Services Information. Other categories can stay unchecked.
apple.step3Body: 1 GB is usually enough. Confirm the request.
apple.step4Body: Apple is preparing your archive. You’ll get an email in a few days.
apple.step5Body: Open Apple’s email and follow the link to your download page.
apple.step6Body: Download each part of the archive. Links expire — save the files somewhere safe.
apple.step7Body: Open each .zip. You should get an Apple_Media_Services folder.
apple.step8Body: In Apple Music Activity, select Apple Music - Play History Daily Tracks.csv — that’s the one to upload here.

insights.subtitle: Understand what each page reveals, how analytics are calculated, and where the current limitations are. Use this as a reference to import data and get more value from the dashboard.

summary.patterns: Patterns: Overview surfaces KPIs plus embedded summaries; Library covers tracks/artists, trend pages, and genre palette; Timeline/heatmap/temporal analysis explore rhythm; AI adds Ask your Soundprint, AI Insights, musical profile, and taste evolution. Account tools (live Spotify, API playground, settings) and the demo videos sit beside that core—they inform or operate the product but do not replace export-backed history.
summary.calculations: Calculations: PostgreSQL aggregations (daily/weekly/monthly), global stats, genre cascade (Track → ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP → Unknown), and CSV/JSON/PDF exports.
summary.limitations: Limitations: Genre mapping coverage, source-data completeness, live Spotify API vs export-backed history, estimated stream time, query performance at scale, and artist/track normalization.
summary.architecture: Architecture: Next.js App Router, PostgreSQL + Prisma, Redis (optional, ioredis) plus TanStack Query, Groq-backed AI with server-side insight caching, Recharts, Spotify/Apple-first ingestion (Last.fm optional).

overview.title: Your Music
overview.paragraph: The /dashboard/overview page is the analytics hub: period, a concrete top-track or top-artist insight, headline KPIs versus the prior window of the same length, one leaderboard for tracks/artists/genres, trend charts behind visible tabs, a heatmap plus AI excerpt, a teaser to Musical Profile, then Chat and Duet. heatmap.paragraph: The /dashboard/heatmap page displays a GitHub-style calendar with streaming intensity per day. It identifies your most active days and distribution by day of the week.

temporal.title: Advanced Temporal Analysis
temporal.paragraph: The /dashboard/temporal-analysis page details your streaming patterns: streams by day of the week (Monday-Sunday), by hour of the day, and identifies peak moments (day and hour when you stream the most).

genres.title: Genre Diversity and Preferences
genres.paragraph: The /dashboard/genres, /dashboard/genres/trends, and /dashboard/genres/palette pages reveal the extent of your musical palette: dominant genres, temporal evolution, diversity metrics, and a dedicated palette visualization. Unique artists and unique tracks highlight the balance between repetition and exploration.

libraryTrends.title: Track and artist trend views
libraryTrends.paragraph: Beyond the high-level genre summaries, /dashboard/tracks/trends and /dashboard/artists/trends chart stream volume across the filtered range using day, week, or month buckets—so you can follow specific tracks or your top artists over time. They honor the same global date filter as the rest of the dashboard.

ai.title: AI-Powered Insights
ai.paragraph: Several experiences use Groq-hosted models on top of your analytics summary and streaming data:
ai.li1: /dashboard/ask-your-soundprint: Conversational assistant with tool-backed answers over your library (honors the dashboard date filter)
ai.li2: /dashboard/ai-insights: Short natural-language insight cards (optional; requires Groq credentials server-side)
ai.li3: /dashboard/musical-profile: Enriches your stats with an AI-generated musical identity
ai.li4: /dashboard/taste-evolution: Week-to-week taste shifts with AI commentary
ai.li5: Repeated AI insight requests reuse a 24h server cache when REDIS_URL is configured (in-memory fallback in local dev) so identical inputs do not always call the model again.

dateRange.title: Date Range Filter
dateRange.paragraph: The top filter scopes analytics to presets (7 days, 30 days, year-to-date, custom range) or all time. For the all-time preset, the client resolves the true min/max stream dates from /api/date-range so features such as AI insights and taste profile use your full history instead of silently falling back to a short default window. Exports (CSV, JSON, PDF) honor the selected range.

accountTooling.title: Account: live Spotify, API playground, and settings
accountTooling.paragraph: The Account section of the sidebar is deliberately separate from the export-backed analytics storyline. /dashboard/spotify-snapshot shows what the Spotify Web API returns today—profile, top tracks and artists, recent streams—so you can compare that live snapshot with the long-term rows in your Stream table built from imports. That route can be used once Spotify is OAuth-linked even when full export onboarding is incomplete; it reflects API state, not your warehouse. /dashboard/spotify-playground is the same family of endpoints in raw JSON form for debugging scopes and payloads; it is operational tooling, not a streaming-history dashboard. /dashboard/settings collects preferences, confirmations, and safety actions (such as deletion): they change your experience and account state, not how historical aggregates are defined from stored streams.

productDemo.title: Walkthrough videos (demo)
productDemo.paragraph: /dashboard/demo embeds product walkthrough videos for orientation and storytelling. Treat them as illustrative—they are not ingested as data, and every personalized chart still derives from streams stored in your account.

aggregations.title: Temporal Aggregations
aggregations.paragraph: Aggregations use native PostgreSQL SQL (via Prisma) for performance:
aggregations.li1: Daily: date bucket from the Stream.playedAt timestamp
aggregations.li2: Weekly: DATE_TRUNC('week', playedAt) buckets ISO weeks (Monday start)
aggregations.li3: Monthly: calendar month bucket from playedAt (typically YYYY-MM)
aggregations.li4: Counts: COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT ...) on streams, tracks, and artists as needed

stats.title: Global Statistics
stats.paragraph: Your Music statistics are calculated as follows:
stats.li1: Total streams: Total count of records in the Stream table
stats.li2: Unique artists: Distinct count of artist_id via streamed tracks
stats.li3: Unique tracks: Distinct count of track_id
stats.li4: Total time: Sum of track durations (in seconds) for all streams

genres.title: Genre Distribution
genres.paragraph: Genres follow a cascade resolution with priority:
genres.li1: 1. Track.genre: Genre stored on the track (from Last.fm when available on import)
genres.li2: 2. ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP: Static manual mapping by artist name (fallback if Track.genre is null)
genres.li4: Streams are aggregated by resolved genre; percentages are calculated on total streams

export.title: Data Export
export.paragraph: Exports are available in the filter bar (CSV, JSON, PDF icons):
export.li1: CSV: All streams with Date, Artist, Title, Genre, Source (period filters applied)
export.li2: JSON: Aggregated statistics (overview, timeline, genres) in structured format
export.li3: PDF: Custom annual report with charts and top artists/tracks per year

genreMapping.title: Genre Mapping
genreMapping.limitation: The ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP fallback only covers a handful of popular artists. Tracks without genre in the database remain classified as "Unknown" when neither Track.genre nor the map provides a value.
genreMapping.impact: Some artists/tracks may appear as "Unknown", reducing the fineness of genre analysis.
genreMapping.solution: Use Last.fm genres when present on imported tracks, or extend ARTIST_TO_GENRE_MAP for additional artists.

dataSources.title: Data Sources
dataSources.limitation: For the public product, primary ingestion is based on user-requested exports (Spotify ZIP + Apple Music CSV). Last.fm remains legacy/optional and is no longer expected in the default UX path.
dataSources.impact: The main risk is missing or stale export files, not missing Last.fm scrobbles. Coverage depends on what users actually request and upload.
dataSources.solution: Design onboarding and in-app prompts around export-import flows; treat Last.fm as an advanced fallback for power users only.

liveSpotifyApi.title: Live Spotify Web API
liveSpotifyApi.limitation: Snapshot and playground calls reflect Spotify's current API rules—time windows, limits, and how "top" or "recent" lists are defined—not the same completeness or replay semantics as a user-requested account export ingested into Stream.
liveSpotifyApi.impact: Side-by-side comparison with your warehouse can diverge (e.g. recency filters, streaming not exposed through these endpoints, curated tops vs. full history in exports).
liveSpotifyApi.solution: Use live API views for debugging or quick checks; rely on imported streams for longitudinal dashboards, exports, and like-for-like historical analysis.

listenTime.title: Stream Time Calculation
listenTime.limitation: Total streaming time is estimated by summing track durations, without accounting for interruptions or partial streams.
listenTime.impact: Calculated time may overestimate actual streaming time if tracks are often interrupted or partially streamed.
listenTime.solution: Possible improvement: Use playback progress data if available in sources.

queryPerformance.title: Query Performance
queryPerformance.limitation: Trade-off: Complex aggregations require loading streams into memory for calculations.
queryPerformance.impact: Performance may degrade with very large datasets (millions of streams).
queryPerformance.solution: Possible optimizations: Materialized views, additional indexes, or asynchronous calculations for large data.

dataNormalization.title: Data Normalization
dataNormalization.limitation: Normalization of artist and track names depends on exact string matching.
dataNormalization.impact: Name variants (e.g. "The Weeknd" vs "Weeknd") may create duplicate entries in statistics.
dataNormalization.solution: Possible improvement: Use MusicBrainz identifiers (MBID) or fuzzy matching algorithms for deduplication.

stack.title: Technology Stack
stack.li1: Backend: Next.js (App Router) with API Routes
stack.li3: Cache: optional Redis (REDIS_URL, ioredis; Upstash-compatible TLS) for AI insight caching plus TanStack Query on the client
stack.li4: Frontend: React 18, TanStack Query v5, Tailwind CSS, Sonner (toasts)
stack.li7: AI/LLM: Groq for generated copy and conversational analytics; insight responses cached server-side (~24h TTL) when Redis is available

model.title: Data Model
model.li1: Artist: name, nameLower (case-insensitive search), MBID, imageUrl
model.li2: Track: title, artist, duration, genre (Last.fm when available), MBID
model.li3: Stream: timestamp (playedAt), source (spotify_export | apple_music_export | apple_music_replay | lastfm), link to Track

import.title: Data Import
import.li1: Primary path (public): user imports from onboarding flows (Spotify export ZIP and Apple Music export CSV), then data is parsed and stored account-side.
import.li2: Secondary path (legacy): Last.fm sync via scripts/API remains available for advanced usage, but is intentionally de-emphasized for UX.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: A plain-language summary of how Soundprint-AI handles your data. We built this app for your Apple Music and Spotify stats — not to sell your information.

sections.title: Who's responsible
paragraphs: Wesley Ajavon (Soundprint-AI) is responsible for your data. Questions? Reach us through account settings or the support channel on the site.

sections.title: What we collect
paragraphs: Only what's needed to run your dashboard:
bullets: Account info — email, name, profile photo, and how you sign in.
Streaming history — artists, tracks, and when you streamed them, from files you upload: an Apple Music CSV export or a Spotify ZIP export.
Spotify connection (optional) — if you sign in with Spotify, we store that link to confirm it works. Your dashboard history still comes from the export you upload, not from a live streaming API.
Your choices — cookie preferences, AI settings, and other consents.
Duet (optional) — if you use friend sharing: relationship status, sharing level you choose, and streaming statistics you allow accepted friends to see.

sections.title: Why we use it
paragraphs: To show your stats from the history you import, keep you signed in, and improve the app. Optional analytics and error reporting only run if you agree in our cookie settings.
AI features that send artist or track names to a provider only run when you opt in.
Duet (friend sharing) only runs when you accept or send a friend request, and only at the sharing level you choose for each friend: comparison and read-only viewing of your stats.

sections.title: How long we keep it
paragraphs: Your account and streaming data stay while your account is active. If you delete your account, we erase your data promptly from our systems.

sections.title: Who we work with
paragraphs: We rely on trusted providers to run the app. They process data only on our instructions and for the purposes below.
bullets: Supabase (hosting, auth, database, profile photo storage) — runs your account and stores your streaming data.
Groq (US) — optional AI features when you opt in; may receive artist/track titles and aggregated streaming stats.
Vercel (global) — hosts the app; optional analytics only if you consent to cookies.
Sentry (US/EU) — optional error monitoring and session replay only if you consent to cookies.

sections.title: Apple Music and Spotify
paragraphs: You request your listening history from Apple or Spotify and upload the file to Soundprint. Apple and Spotify are not our processors for that export — we only receive what you choose to upload.
If you optionally sign in with Spotify, Spotify’s rules apply to that connection. Soundprint-AI isn’t affiliated with Apple or Spotify.

sections.title: International transfers
paragraphs: Some providers may process data outside your country (including the United States). When required, we rely on appropriate safeguards such as the providers' data processing agreements and standard contractual clauses.
Groq and Sentry are only used for the optional features described above and only when you opt in (AI) or accept the relevant cookies.

sections.title: Sharing with friends (Duet)
paragraphs: Duet lets you compare streaming statistics with friends who have a Soundprint-AI account, and view an accepted friend’s stats dashboard (Your Music) read-only, at the sharing level they chose. This feature is entirely optional.

To see another user's stats, you must send them a friend request (by email) or accept theirs. They choose whether to accept and what to share: aggregated statistics (trends, top artists and genres — no track list) that can be viewed and compared; or, if they choose detailed sharing, the same aggregates plus top tracks and head-to-head comparisons for an artist, track, or genre.

What you share is decided by you, friend by friend, when you accept a request. You can change the sharing level or revoke a friend anytime in Settings → Duet sharing. We record your consent (type and version) as proof.
We do not offer public user discovery, an activity feed, or open leaderboards. Your email is not shown to friends in Duet. Invitations use a uniform response to limit account enumeration.

sections.title: Your rights
paragraphs: You can access, export, correct, or delete your data. Go to Settings → Data & privacy to export or delete your account.
You can also change cookie, AI, and Duet sharing choices anytime. If you're in the EU, you may contact your local data protection authority.
